questions.stem: Examine the description of the SALES table and the statement below. Which two statements are true?

codeBlocks.title: SQL statement
codeBlocks.code:
CREATE TABLE sales1 (
prod_id, cust_id, quantity_sold, price
)
AS
SELECT product_id, customer_id, quantity_sold, price
FROM sales
WHERE 1 = 1;

options.text: SALES1 is created with 1 row.
options.explanation: The condition 1 = 1 is true for all 55,000 source rows, not just one row.

options.text: SALES1 is created with no rows.
options.explanation: The query does not contain a false condition such as WHERE 1 = 0.

options.text: SALES1 is created with 55,000 rows.
options.explanation: All rows from the SALES table satisfy the condition and are copied into SALES1.

options.text: SALES1 has NOT NULL constraints on any selected columns that had those constraints in the SALES table.
options.explanation: The selected source columns are direct column references, so their explicitly defined NOT NULL properties are carried into the new table.

options.text: SALES1 has a primary key and unique constraints on selected columns that had those constraints in the SALES table.
options.explanation: A CREATE TABLE AS SELECT operation does not copy primary-key or unique constraints from the source table.

questions.answerExplanation: All rows from the SALES table satisfy the condition and are copied into SALES1. The selected source columns are direct column references, so their explicitly defined NOT NULL properties are carried into the new table.
questions.technicalNote: The missing statement that SALES contains 55,000 rows was restored from the correction document. It is required to evaluate the CTAS result.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the EMP table and the query below. What is the result?

codeBlocks.title: Query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT deptno AS "departments",
SUM(sal) AS "salary"
FROM emp
GROUP BY 1
HAVING SUM(sal) > 3000;

options.text: Only departments where the total salary is greater than 3000, ordered by department.
options.explanation: The query does not contain an ORDER BY clause. More importantly, the positional reference in GROUP BY 1 is not accepted by the Oracle version targeted by this question.

options.text: An error.
options.explanation: In the Oracle SQL version covered by this reviewer, a select-list position cannot replace the grouping expression in GROUP BY. It should use GROUP BY deptno.

options.text: All departments and a sum of the employees with a salary greater than 3000.
options.explanation: HAVING SUM(sal) > 3000 filters department groups based on total salary. It does not filter individual employees whose salary exceeds 3000.

options.text: Only departments where the total salary is greater than 3000, returned in no particular order.
options.explanation: This would describe the intended result if the query used GROUP BY deptno, but the displayed query produces an error.

questions.answerExplanation: In the Oracle SQL version covered by this reviewer, a select-list position cannot replace the grouping expression in GROUP BY. It should use GROUP BY deptno.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the EMPLOYEES table and the failing statement below. Which clause causes the error?

codeBlocks.title: Failing statement
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT dept_no AS department_id,
MAX(salary) AS max_sal
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 10000
GROUP BY department_id
ORDER BY max_sal;

options.text: SELECT
options.explanation: Selecting the department number and an aggregate value is valid when the department expression is grouped correctly.

options.text: ORDER BY
options.explanation: A select-list alias such as max_sal can be referenced in the ORDER BY clause.

options.text: GROUP BY
options.explanation: The query uses the select-list alias department_id in GROUP BY. In this Oracle SQL context, it must use the underlying column: GROUP BY dept_no.

options.text: WHERE
options.explanation: Filtering individual employee rows with WHERE salary > 10000 before grouping is valid.

questions.answerExplanation: The query uses the select-list alias department_id in GROUP BY. In this Oracle SQL context, it must use the underlying column: GROUP BY dept_no.

questions.stem: Examine this statement, which returns the name of each employee and the employee’s manager. You want to extend the query to include managers with no employees. What must you add before JOIN to do this?

codeBlocks.title: Existing query
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT e.last_name AS emp, m.last_name AS mgr
FROM employees e JOIN managers m
ON e.manager_id = m.manager_id
ORDER BY emp;

options.text: LEFT OUTER
options.explanation: A left outer join preserves every employee row from the left side, not every manager row from the right side.

options.text: FULL OUTER
options.explanation: A full outer join preserves unmatched rows from both sides. That is broader than the stated requirement.

options.text: RIGHT OUTER
options.explanation: A right outer join preserves every manager row, including managers with no matching employees.

options.text: CROSS
options.explanation: A cross join produces every possible employee-manager combination and does not use the relationship to identify the correct manager.

questions.answerExplanation: A right outer join preserves every manager row, including managers with no matching employees.
questions.technicalNote: The existing query is now displayed as one SQL block. The earlier analysis that revealed which side had to be preserved was removed from the question body.

questions.stem: The ORDER_ITEMS table contains ORDER_ID, UNIT_PRICE, and QUANTITY, all with the NUMBER data type. Examine the two statements below. Which two statements are true?

sections.title: Table information
sections.content: ORDER_ITEMS contains ORDER_ID, UNIT_PRICE, and QUANTITY. All three columns use the NUMBER data type.

codeBlocks.title: Statement 1
codeBlocks.code:
SELECT MAX(unit_price * quantity) "Maximum Order"
FROM order_items;

codeBlocks.title: Statement 2

options.text: Statement 1 returns only one row of output.
options.explanation: Without GROUP BY, the aggregate function treats all rows as one group and returns one maximum value.

options.text: Statement 2 returns only one row of output.
options.explanation: Statement 2 can return one row for every distinct ORDER_ID.

options.text: Both statements give the same output.
options.explanation: Statement 1 returns an overall maximum, while Statement 2 returns a maximum for each order.

options.text: Statement 2 may return multiple rows of output.
options.explanation: Each distinct order ID forms a separate group, so multiple order IDs produce multiple result rows.

options.text: Both statements will return NULL if either UNIT_PRICE or QUANTITY contains NULL.
options.explanation: A null multiplication result is ignored by MAX when other non-null expression results exist. MAX returns null only when all evaluated values in the relevant group are null.

questions.answerExplanation: Without GROUP BY, the aggregate function treats all rows as one group and returns one maximum value. Each distinct order ID forms a separate group, so multiple order IDs produce multiple result rows.
questions.technicalNote: Statement 1 and Statement 2 were restored as separate SQL blocks. The earlier embedded analysis of their row counts was removed from the question body.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the PRODUCT_INFORMATION table. Which query retrieves the number of products with a null list price?

options.explanation: Null values must be tested with IS NULL, not = NULL. In addition, COUNT(list_price) does not count null values.
The WHERE clause selects rows with null list prices. NVL converts each null to zero, allowing COUNT to count every selected row.
COUNT(DISTINCT list_price) excludes nulls, so it returns zero for rows selected by LIST_PRICE IS NULL.
Although the filter correctly selects null list prices, COUNT(list_price) ignores those null values and returns zero.

questions.answerExplanation: The WHERE clause selects rows with null list prices. NVL converts each null to zero, allowing COUNT to count every selected row.

questions.stem: The SYSDATE function displays the current Oracle server date as 21-MAY-19. You want to display the date as MONDAY, 21 MAY, 2019. Which statement will do this?

sections.title: Current display
sections.content:
2019-05-21 00:00:00
This is the current date displayed using the existing date format.

sections.title: Required display
sections.content:
MONDAY, 21 MAY, 2019
The output requires the complete day name, two-digit day, full uppercase month name, and four-digit year.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'FMDAY DDTH MONTH, YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: DDTH adds an ordinal suffix, such as 21ST, which is not part of the required output.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'FMDAY, DD MONTH, YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: DAY returns the day name, DD returns the day number, MONTH returns the complete month name, and YYYY returns the four-digit year. FM removes unwanted blank padding.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(SYSDATE, 'FMDAY, DD MONTH, YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: TO_DATE converts character data to a date. It is not used to format a date for display.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(SYSDATE, 'FMDAY, DAY MONTH, YYYY') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The second DAY returns another day name instead of the numeric day of the month.

questions.answerExplanation: DAY returns the day name, DD returns the day number, MONTH returns the complete month name, and YYYY returns the four-digit year. FM removes unwanted blank padding.

questions.stem: Examine this SQL statement. Which two statements are true?

codeBlocks.title: SQL statement
codeBlocks.code:
DELETE FROM employees e
WHERE EXISTS
(SELECT 'dummy'
FROM emp_history
WHERE employee_id = e.employee_id);

options.text: The DELETE statement executes successfully even if the subquery selects multiple rows.
options.explanation: EXISTS checks only whether at least one matching row exists. It does not require the subquery to return exactly one row.

options.text: The subquery is executed before the DELETE statement is executed.
options.explanation: The correlated subquery is evaluated in relation to each candidate row processed by the outer statement.

options.text: The subquery is executed for every row in the EMPLOYEES table.
options.explanation: Because the subquery references the current employee row, the matching condition is evaluated for each candidate row in EMPLOYEES.

options.text: All existing rows in the EMPLOYEES table are deleted.
options.explanation: Only employees with at least one corresponding EMP_HISTORY row are deleted.

options.text: The subquery is not a correlated subquery.
options.explanation: The reference to e.employee_id correlates the subquery with the outer EMPLOYEES row.

questions.answerExplanation: EXISTS checks only whether at least one matching row exists. It does not require the subquery to return exactly one row. Because the subquery references the current employee row, the matching condition is evaluated for each candidate row in EMPLOYEES.

questions.stem: Which two statements execute successfully?

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR(TO_DATE('2019-DEC-25 03:30', 'YYYY-MON-DD HH12:MI')) FROM dual;
options.explanation: The input uses a 12-hour time value of 03:30, which is compatible with HH12:MI. TO_DATE converts it to a date, and TO_CHAR converts the result to character output.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE(TO_CHAR('2019-DEC-25 03:30', 'YYYY-MON-DD HH12:MI')) FROM dual;
options.explanation: TO_CHAR is being applied to a character literal with a date format model. Oracle cannot directly treat that character value as the required date input in this expression.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR('2019-DEC-25 15:30', 'YYYY-MON-DD HH24:MI') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The first argument is a character literal, not a date or timestamp value. It must first be converted using TO_DATE.

options.text: SELECT TO_DATE('2019-DEC-25 15:30', 'YYYY-MON-DD HH24:MI', 'NLS_DATE_LANGUAGE = AMERICAN') FROM dual;
options.explanation: The date string matches the format model, 15 is valid with HH24, and the NLS parameter specifies the language used to interpret DEC.

options.text: SELECT TO_CHAR('2019-DEC-25 15:30', 'YYYY-MON-DD HH24:MI', 'NLS_DATE_LANGUAGE = AMERICAN') FROM dual;
options.explanation: TO_CHAR does not convert the displayed character literal into a date. The input must first be a date or timestamp value.

questions.answerExplanation: The input uses a 12-hour time value of 03:30, which is compatible with HH12:MI. TO_DATE converts it to a date, and TO_CHAR converts the result to character output. The date string matches the format model, 15 is valid with HH24, and the NLS parameter specifies the language used to interpret DEC.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about single-row functions?

options.text: The argument can be a column name, variable, literal, or an expression.
options.explanation: A single-row function can accept different kinds of expressions as arguments, including columns, literals, variables, and calculated expressions.

options.text: They can accept only one argument.
options.explanation: Some single-row functions accept one argument, while others accept two or more arguments.

options.text: They return a single result row per table.
options.explanation: A single-row function returns one result for each row processed, not one result for the entire table.

options.text: The data type returned can be different from the data type of the argument.
options.explanation: A conversion function can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a date or number into character data.

options.text: They can be nested to any level.
options.explanation: The output of one single-row function can be supplied as the argument of another function.

options.text: They can be used only in the WHERE clause of SELECT statements.
options.explanation: Single-row functions can be used in several clauses, including SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY.

questions.answerExplanation: A single-row function can accept different kinds of expressions as arguments, including columns, literals, variables, and calculated expressions. A conversion function can accept one data type and return another, such as TO_CHAR converting a date or number into character data. The output of one single-row function can be supplied as the argument of another function.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about an ORDER BY clause?

options.text: By default, an ORDER BY clause sorts rows in descending order.
options.explanation: The default sorting direction is ascending. Descending order requires the DESC keyword.

options.text: An ORDER BY clause can perform a binary sort.
options.explanation: Character values can be ordered according to their binary character values.

options.text: By default, an ORDER BY clause sorts rows in ascending order.
options.explanation: Oracle uses ascending order when neither ASC nor DESC is specified.

options.text: An ORDER BY clause can perform a linguistic sort.
options.explanation: Oracle can sort character data using linguistic rules determined by applicable globalization settings or functions.

options.text: An ORDER BY clause always sorts null values last.
options.explanation: Null placement depends on the sorting direction. It can also be controlled explicitly with NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST.

options.text: An ORDER BY clause will always precede a HAVING clause if both are used in the same top-level query.
options.explanation: HAVING appears before ORDER BY in SQL statement syntax.

questions.answerExplanation: Character values can be ordered according to their binary character values. Oracle uses ascending order when neither ASC nor DESC is specified. Oracle can sort character data using linguistic rules determined by applicable globalization settings or functions.

questions.stem: Examine the data in the ORDERS and INVOICES tables and the query below. Which three rows will be returned?

FROM orders
MINUS
SELECT order_id, order_date
FROM invoices;

options.explanation: The same complete row appears in both tables, so MINUS removes it.
INVOICES has a null date for order 5, not 01-MAR-2019, so the ORDERS row remains.
INVOICES has a null date for order 3, so the complete ORDERS row does not have a match.

options.text: 3, NULL
options.explanation: This row appears only in INVOICES and therefore cannot be returned from ORDERS MINUS INVOICES.

options.text: 2, NULL
options.explanation: INVOICES contains order 2 with 01-JAN-2019, not a null date, so the complete row remains.

options.text: 1, NULL
options.explanation: The same complete row appears in both tables and is removed by MINUS.

questions.stem: Examine the sequence of statements below. Which three statements are true?

codeBlocks.title: Statements executed

options.text: There is no row containing pen.
options.explanation: The deletion of the row with code 10 occurs after savepoint B and is reversed by ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT b.

options.text: There is no row containing fountain pen.
options.explanation: The rollback reverses the update from code 3 to code 30, restoring the fountain-pen row with code 3.

options.text: The code for pen is 1.
options.explanation: The update from code 1 to code 10 was committed before savepoint B was established.

options.explanation: The later update to code 30 is undone by the rollback to savepoint B.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about TRUNCATE and DELETE?

options.text: The result of a TRUNCATE can be undone by issuing a ROLLBACK.
options.explanation: TRUNCATE is a DDL statement that causes an implicit commit. Its result cannot normally be reversed with ROLLBACK.

options.text: TRUNCATE leaves any indexes on the table in an UNUSABLE state.
options.explanation: Indexes associated with a truncated table remain usable. Oracle removes the index data while preserving the index definitions.

options.text: The result of a DELETE can be undone by issuing a ROLLBACK.
options.explanation: DELETE is a DML statement. Its uncommitted changes can be reversed using ROLLBACK.

options.text: TRUNCATE can use a WHERE clause to determine which rows should be removed.
options.explanation: TRUNCATE removes all rows from the table and does not support a WHERE clause. Use DELETE to remove selected rows.

options.text: DELETE can use a WHERE clause to determine which rows should be removed.
options.explanation: A WHERE clause allows DELETE to remove only rows satisfying the specified condition. Without WHERE, all rows are deleted.

questions.answerExplanation: DELETE is a DML statement. Its uncommitted changes can be reversed using ROLLBACK. A WHERE clause allows DELETE to remove only rows satisfying the specified condition. Without WHERE, all rows are deleted.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true about the WHERE and HAVING clauses in a SELECT statement?

options.text: The WHERE clause can be used to exclude rows before dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: Oracle applies the WHERE condition to individual rows before processing GROUP BY.

options.text: Aggregating functions and columns used in HAVING clauses must be specified in the SELECT clause of a query.
options.explanation: An aggregate expression can be used in HAVING even when that expression is not displayed in the select list.

options.text: The HAVING clause can be used with aggregating functions in subqueries.
options.explanation: A subquery may contain grouping and a HAVING clause that filters its aggregate results.

options.text: The WHERE clause can be used to exclude rows after dividing them into groups.
options.explanation: WHERE operates before grouping. Grouped results are filtered with HAVING.

options.text: WHERE and HAVING clauses can be used in the same statement only if applied to different columns.
options.explanation: Both clauses may reference the same column when appropriate. Their distinction is based on processing stage, not whether they reference different columns.

questions.answerExplanation: Oracle applies the WHERE condition to individual rows before processing GROUP BY. A subquery may contain grouping and a HAVING clause that filters its aggregate results.

questions.stem: Examine the description of the TRANSACTION table. Which two SQL statements execute successfully?

options.explanation: This statement does not execute because single quotation marks create character literals, not delimited aliases. Aliases such as CUSTOMER-ID or DUES must use double quotation marks when special characters or preserved case are required.

options.text: SELECT customer_id CUSTID, transaction_date TRANS_DATE, amount + 100 DUES FROM transactions;
options.explanation: This statement executes. CUSTID, TRANS_DATE, and DUES are valid unquoted aliases made from letters and underscores, and AS is optional for column aliases.

options.text: SELECT customer_id AS 'CUSTOMER-ID', transaction_date AS TRANS_DATE, amount + 100 "DUES_AMOUNT" FROM transactions;
options.explanation: This choice is highlighted by the reviewer, but the single-quoted CUSTOMER-ID is technically not a valid column alias in Oracle SQL. The conflict is documented in the technical note.

options.text: SELECT customer_id AS "CUSTOMER-ID", transaction_date AS DATE, amount + 100 "DUES" FROM transactions;
options.explanation: The quoted aliases are valid, but DATE is used as an unquoted alias. The reviewer does not select this statement; use a nonreserved alias or delimit the alias consistently.

options.text: SELECT customer_id AS "CUSTOMER-ID", transaction_date AS "DATE", amount + 100 DUES FROM transactions;
options.explanation: This statement executes. Double quotes correctly delimit CUSTOMER-ID and DATE, while DUES is a valid unquoted alias.

questions.answerExplanation: This statement executes. CUSTID, TRANS_DATE, and DUES are valid unquoted aliases made from letters and underscores, and AS is optional for column aliases. This choice is highlighted by the reviewer, but the single-quoted CUSTOMER-ID is technically not a valid column alias in Oracle SQL. The conflict is documented in the technical note. This statement executes. Double quotes correctly delimit CUSTOMER-ID and DATE, while DUES is a valid unquoted alias.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about aggregate functions?

options.text: The MAX and MIN functions can be used on columns with character data types.
options.explanation: MAX and MIN can evaluate character values according to the applicable character sorting rules.

options.text: The AVG function implicitly converts nulls to zero.
options.explanation: AVG ignores null values. It does not include them as zero when calculating the average.

options.text: Aggregate functions can be used in any clause of a SELECT statement.
options.explanation: Aggregate functions cannot normally be used directly in clauses such as WHERE. Aggregate conditions belong in HAVING.

options.text: Aggregate functions can be nested to any number of levels.
options.explanation: Aggregate-function nesting is subject to SQL syntax and query-level restrictions. It is not unlimited.

questions.answerExplanation: MAX and MIN can evaluate character values according to the applicable character sorting rules.

questions.stem: Which three statements are true about the MERGE statement?

options.text: It can update, insert, or delete rows conditionally in multiple tables.
options.explanation: The source reviewer highlights this statement. However, a standard Oracle MERGE has one target table, so the phrase “in multiple tables” makes the wording technically questionable.

options.text: It can merge rows only from tables.
options.explanation: The USING source may be a table, view, or subquery rather than only a base table.

options.text: It can combine rows from multiple tables conditionally to insert into a single table.
options.explanation: The source reviewer does not select this choice. A source subquery can nevertheless join multiple tables, so the wording may be interpreted as technically possible.

options.text: It can use subqueries to produce source rows.
options.explanation: The USING clause can contain a subquery whose result supplies the source rows for the merge.

options.text: It can update the same row of the target table multiple times.
options.explanation: A deterministic MERGE operation cannot update the same target row more than once within one statement.

options.text: It can use views to produce source rows.
options.explanation: A view can be used as the source row set in the USING clause.

questions.answerExplanation: The source reviewer highlights this statement. However, a standard Oracle MERGE has one target table, so the phrase “in multiple tables” makes the wording technically questionable. The USING clause can contain a subquery whose result supplies the source rows for the merge. A view can be used as the source row set in the USING clause.

questions.stem: Which is the default column or columns for sorting output from compound queries using INTERSECT in a SQL statement?

options.text: The first column in the last SELECT of the compound query
options.explanation: The output column definitions, including the names used by the final ORDER BY, come from the first SELECT.

options.text: The first NUMBER column in the first SELECT of the compound query
options.explanation: Oracle does not automatically select the first numeric column as the sorting column.

options.text: The first VARCHAR2 column in the first SELECT of the compound query
options.explanation: The data type does not determine the default sorting column.

options.text: The first NUMBER or VARCHAR2 column in the last SELECT of the compound query
options.explanation: The last component query does not determine the compound query’s default output column definitions.

options.text: The first column in the first SELECT of the compound query
options.explanation: The compound query’s output columns are determined by the first SELECT. In the context of this question, the first output column is the expected sorting column.

questions.answerExplanation: The compound query’s output columns are determined by the first SELECT. In the context of this question, the first output column is the expected sorting column.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about the INTERSECT operator used in compound queries?

options.text: INTERSECT has lower precedence than UNION or UNION ALL.
options.explanation: In the Oracle SQL behavior covered by this reviewer, set operators have equal precedence and are evaluated from left to right unless parentheses alter the evaluation order.

options.text: It ignores nulls.
options.explanation: Null values participate in set comparisons. Corresponding null values can be considered equal during a set operation.

options.text: Multiple INTERSECT operators are not possible in the same SQL statement.
options.explanation: Multiple set operators, including multiple INTERSECT operators, can be used in one compound query.

options.text: It processes nulls in the selected columns.
options.explanation: INTERSECT compares complete selected rows, including corresponding null values, to identify rows common to both query results.

questions.answerExplanation: INTERSECT compares complete selected rows, including corresponding null values, to identify rows common to both query results.

questions.stem: The ORDER table has an ORDER_DATE column with the DATE data type. The default date format is RR. Which two WHERE conditions demonstrate the correct use of conversion functions?

questions.stem: You need to calculate the number of days from January 1, 2019 until today. Dates are stored in the default format DD-MON-RR. Which two queries give the required output?

questions.stem: Examine the description of the PRODUCT_STATUS table. The STATUS column contains either IN STOCK or OUT OF STOCK for each row. Which two queries execute successfully?

options.explanation: The alternative-quoted text and quoted column alias are syntactically valid, so the statement executes. The OUT OF STOCKS filter matches no stated rows, but returning no rows is not an execution error.

options.text: SELECT prod_id || q'[ ('s not available) ]' "CURRENT AVAILABILITY" FROM product_status WHERE status = 'OUT OF STOCK';
options.explanation: This statement executes and can return the out-of-stock rows. The q-quoted text is valid, CURRENT AVAILABILITY is a valid quoted alias, and the filter matches the stated status value.

options.text: SELECT prod_id || q'[ ('s not available) ]' FROM product_status WHERE status = 'OUT OF STOCKS';

questions.stem: Examine the description of the MEMBERS table and the partial query. You want to display all cities containing the string AN, sorted by city in ascending order and then by last name in descending order. Which two clauses must you add?

SELECT city, last_name AS lname
FROM members ...;

options.text: ORDER BY 1, 2
options.explanation: Both columns would use ascending order by default, but the last name must be sorted in descending order.

options.text: ORDER BY 1, lname DESC
options.explanation: Position 1 sorts CITY in ascending order by default, and LNAME DESC sorts matching last names in descending order.

options.text: WHERE city IN ('%AN%')
options.explanation: IN performs equality comparison and does not interpret % as a wildcard.

options.text: WHERE city = '%A%'
options.explanation: The equality operator treats % as a literal character rather than as a wildcard.

options.text: WHERE city LIKE '%AN%'
options.explanation: LIKE interprets % as a wildcard and finds city values containing AN anywhere in the text.

options.text: ORDER BY last_name DESC, city ASC
options.explanation: This sorts by last name first, but the requirement is to sort primarily by city.

questions.answerExplanation: Position 1 sorts CITY in ascending order by default, and LNAME DESC sorts matching last names in descending order. LIKE interprets % as a wildcard and finds city values containing AN anywhere in the text.
